clinicalPearls: FKTN encodes fukutin, a ribitol-phosphate transferase in the alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation pathway; its deficiency produces the classic dystroglycanopathy loss of laminin-binding glycan.
A founder retrotransposon insertion in FKTN makes Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy one of the commonest muscular dystrophies in the Japanese population.
Fukuyama disease presents in infancy with hypotonia, weakness, contractures, intellectual disability, seizures and a raised creatine kinase.
Brain MRI shows cobblestone (type II) cortical malformation, frequently with polymicrogyria, cerebellar cysts and white-matter change.
FKTN variants also cause Walker-Warburg syndrome and muscle-eye-brain-like disease at the severe end of the spectrum.
Distinct milder FKTN phenotypes include a limb-girdle muscular dystrophy and a dilated cardiomyopathy that can occur with relatively preserved skeletal muscle strength.
Muscle immunohistochemistry demonstrates reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan with intact core protein, as in other dystroglycanopathies.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive; cardiac surveillance is important because cardiomyopathy may dominate or emerge over time.
reference.pathophysiology: FKTN encodes fukutin, a Golgi-resident enzyme that acts as a ribitol-5-phosphate transferase in the biosynthesis of the matriglycan on alpha-dystroglycan. Together with the related enzyme fukutin-related protein and other components of the O-mannosylation pathway, fukutin builds the tandem ribitol-phosphate linker onto which the repeating xylose-glucuronic acid matriglycan is assembled; this glycan is what binds laminin and other extracellular-matrix ligands. Biallelic pathogenic FKTN variants (including the characteristic founder insertion causing Fukuyama disease) impair this step, leaving alpha-dystroglycan hypoglycosylated and unable to link the muscle sarcolemma and the cerebral glia-limitans to the basement membrane. In skeletal muscle this produces a dystrophic process; in the developing brain the disrupted glia-limitans allows neuronal overmigration and cobblestone cortical malformation; and in the heart deficient glycosylation contributes to a dilated cardiomyopathy. Residual enzyme activity governs whether the phenotype is a severe congenital brain-eye-muscle disorder or a milder limb-girdle or cardiac-predominant presentation.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic causes of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy
Congenital myopathies presenting with neonatal hypotonia
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI for cobblestone malformation, cerebellar cysts and white-matter change
Echocardiography and electrocardiography for cardiomyopathy and conduction disease
Muscle biopsy with glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan immunohistochemistry
Molecular testing of FKTN including assessment for the founder insertion where relevant
Genetic counselling and family carrier testing
redFlags: Signs of heart failure or arrhythmia from dilated cardiomyopathy
Respiratory muscle weakness with hypoventilation or recurrent chest infection
Rapid loss of motor milestones or feeding ability in infancy
Deteriorating vision in severe brain-eye-muscle presentations
reference.prognosis: Walker-Warburg and Fukuyama presentations carry a poor prognosis with early disability and reduced survival, seizures and cognitive impairment. Milder limb-girdle and cardiac-predominant forms vary widely, and cardiomyopathy can be a major determinant of outcome even when skeletal weakness is mild.
pitfalls: Focusing on skeletal weakness and missing an evolving dilated cardiomyopathy that may dominate the FKTN phenotype.
Assuming the diagnosis is excluded by a normal alpha-dystroglycan core protein when the defect is in glycosylation.
Not testing specifically for the founder insertion in patients of relevant ancestry when standard sequencing is uninformative.
Confusing FKTN with FKRP disease, which is a separate gene with an overlapping but distinct spectrum.
Omitting cardiac surveillance in apparently mild or limb-girdle cases.
references: Standard textbooks of paediatric neurology and neuromuscular disease
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; care is supportive and multidisciplinary
Physiotherapy, stretching and orthoses to preserve mobility and prevent contractures
Surveillance and treatment of dilated cardiomyopathy with heart-failure therapy such as ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers
Respiratory monitoring with non-invasive ventilation for hypoventilation
Antiepileptic drugs for seizures and educational support for intellectual disability
Regular cardiac (echocardiography and ECG) and neurological surveillance
Ophthalmological review and broader specialist input in severe presentations
Genetic counselling and family testing for this autosomal recessive disorder, including the founder insertion where relevant
